source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2
finding: 28 findings replicated in 125 samples. Half held up under the strict test. The typical effect shrank to a quarter of the original size.
numbers: 15,305 participants, 36 countries. 15 of 28 (54%) significant in the same direction at p<.05; 14 (50%) at p<.0001. Median d: original 0.60, replication 0.15. 57% had d<.20; 32% went the opposite way. 25% of replications had larger effects than the original.
limits: Mostly social and judgment findings, not all H&B. Online and lab samples.
agent_relevance: Base rate for any single classic effect: about even odds that the original size holds. Treat any one bias as a hint, not a law.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: incidental anchors (Critcher & Gilovich 2008)
finding: The incidental anchor (a phone named P97 vs P17) did not replicate.
numbers: Original N=207: 58.1% vs 51.9% sales estimate, d=0.30. Replication N=6,826: 49.87% vs 48.98%, d=0.04, 95% CI [-0.01,0.09]. Paper-and-pencil sites (N=1,112): d=-0.01.
limits: Incidental, irrelevant numbers are the weak kind of anchor. Contrast with explicit comparison anchors, which are large (b05, b06).
agent_relevance: Irrelevant numbers sitting in context are low risk for S1 hygiene. Numbers the model must compare against are high risk.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: Tversky & Kahneman 1981 framing (cheap item vs costly item, $5 saving)
finding: A Tversky-Kahneman (1981, Study 10) framing result replicated, but at under half the original strength.
limits: This is the shop-saving problem, not the Asian disease problem. Items and prices were updated for 2014.
agent_relevance: Context-relative valuation is real but smaller than first reported.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: heterogeneity
finding: Differences between effects mattered more than differences between sites. Large effects varied most across settings.
numbers: 11 of 28 (39%) showed significant heterogeneity (Q); 10 (36%) had I2>=50%. Only one near-zero effect was heterogeneous.
limits: WEIRD vs non-WEIRD split gave similar medians.
agent_relevance: Expect the effect to depend on the item more than on the person. Test the agent per item type.

source: Kakinohana, Pilati & Klein (2023) Does anchoring vary across cultures?
finding: Anchoring is large in all four Many Labs tasks, but varies a lot by country. Cultural values explain some of that.
numbers: N=6,344 in ten countries plus Many Labs data. Effect (r): NYC distance 0.26 [.22,.31] I2=64.6%; Chicago 0.48 I2=86.8%; Everest 0.61 [.56,.65] I2=87.3%; babies born 0.57 [.52,.61] I2=82.7%. Intellectual Autonomy and Egalitarianism negatively related to effect size; Harmony negative (largest share of heterogeneity); Mastery positive.
limits: Country-level correlations with about 36 sites; not causal. Pre-registered, but pre-peer-review version read.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is a robust core effect with a moving size. Items with a familiar true scale (distance) show a smaller pull than open-ended ones.

source: Schley & Weingarten (2026) A metastudy on anchoring effect moderators
finding: A large preregistered test of eight moderators in the classic high-vs-low anchor task. Anchors moved estimates by over half a standard deviation.
numbers: N=1,967 US adults, 8 general-knowledge questions. High anchors shifted estimates +0.57 item SDs. Debiasing reminder: 0.613 to 0.499. Cognitive load: 0.513 to 0.597. Subjective knowledge: 0.641 (-1 SD), 0.555 (mean), 0.470 (+1 SD). Incentive 0.550 vs none 0.560.
limits: Draft, not peer reviewed. Online letter-memory load is light. One paradigm only.
agent_relevance: A warning alone cuts the pull by about 18% but never removes it. A small accuracy incentive does nothing. Do not rely on 'ignore the anchor' text.

source: Schley & Weingarten (2026) metastudy: distance and relevance
finding: Anchors pull harder when they apply to the target judgment and sit farther from the centre of what people already believe. The effect grows steadily with anchor distance.
numbers: Effect rose monotonically with anchor distance in the 8-question design; directionality, trailing decimals and page breaks produced little evidence of moderation. Text cites a prior meta-analysis (not opened) of hundreds of studies robust to publication-bias correction.
limits: Draft. The cognitive-load and calibrated-extremity results diverge from the earlier meta-analysis, so some moderators are unsettled.
agent_relevance: Strip needless reference numbers from the prompt. Remove anchor values that match the judgment target.

source: Rebholz et al. (2026 registered report) Assimilation to external cues: reliability of anchoring, advice taking, hindsight bias
finding: Anchoring is a robust group effect but a poor individual-difference measure. Advice taking is very reliable.
numbers: Study 1 (open data): split-half reliability lowest for anchoring ('not reliable'), moderate for hindsight, highest for advice taking (r=.96 cited for algorithmic advice). Prior hindsight reliability r=.11 (Pohl 1999) to r=.56-.91 (Gross 2022).
limits: Stage 1 registered report; Study 2 data not yet collected.
agent_relevance: Anchoring susceptibility varies noisily by item for the same person; sample many items and many runs before calling an agent biased.

source: DeKay (2025) Risky-choice framing effects persist when option descriptions are matched and complete
finding: The gain-loss risky-choice framing effect partly comes from mismatched wording, but a smaller effect stays even for matched, complete descriptions.
numbers: Replication N=1,697 (census-matched), 477 on completely described options. Complete-option framing effect b=0.61, 95% CI [0.29,0.93], OR=1.84, p<.001; significant in 3 of 4 domains. Framing effects significant in 7 of 9 matched comparisons.
limits: Replicates DeKay & Dou (2024; 18 option pairs). Only a rescaled explicated-valence account fits all samples; fuzzy-trace and prospect theory fit less.
agent_relevance: Framing risk comes from wording that signals good or bad (valence), so rewrite input to neutral, complete, matched wording.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of LLMs via human cognitive biases: irrelevant preceding function
finding: Codex and CodeGen copy irrelevant prompt content. Accuracy collapsed when an irrelevant function was put before the task.
numbers: HumanEval, Codex accuracy 32.9% original vs 2.4-10.6% framed (drop 22.3-30.5 points); CodeGen 25.6% vs 1.5-11.0%. Framing line appeared in output 81% (Codex) and 70.7% (CodeGen) vs 4.5% and 0.0% on untransformed prompts.
limits: Old code models (davinci-001, CodeGen 6.2B), greedy decoding. A copying artifact more than a pure framing effect.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant text in context is copied or leaned on. Keep S1 input clean.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022): anchoring in Codex and GPT-3
finding: Code models adjust toward anchor lines in the prompt. GPT-3 moves estimates toward an anchor (Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 design).
numbers: Codex writes the anchor line 'return tmp' in 26-46% of solutions, CodeGen 13-79%; verbatim copy of the whole anchor function only 7-12% (Codex). GPT-3 estimate shifts toward anchor 28.6% (p=20%) and 42.9% (p=50%), away 10.7%, no change 10.7-14.3%, gibberish 50.0% and 32.1%.
limits: Small question set; 41% average gibberish outputs; templated prompts.
agent_relevance: Anchor effects exist in base models; a quarter to half of outputs shifted.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022): Asian disease framing in GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 mirrors the Asian disease reversal, with a boundary: when the save probability is high, both frames choose the risky option.
numbers: 704 prompts, option order and labels varied. Risky choice: save frame 28% (humans, 1981) vs 45% (GPT-3); die frame 78% (humans) vs 74% (GPT-3). At save probability 1/3: 11.3% save frame vs 60.0% die frame.
limits: Appendix result; no human sample run by the authors.
agent_relevance: LLMs show the gain-loss flip. Keep input and output frames matched.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 gave the human answer on the Linda problem but not on the cab problem. Small changes to a problem broke it.
numbers: 12 vignette tasks: 6 correct, all 12 human-like. Linda: conjunction fallacy shown. Cab: base rate used. GPT-3 showed three of six prospect-theory biases (framing, certainty, overweighting of small probabilities). Black-cab variant (should be near 0) gave '20%'; reordered Wason card list failed.
limits: Famous vignettes are probably in training data. Authors say vignette results alone do not show human-likeness.
agent_relevance: Use perturbed variants. A pass on a textbook item says little.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Intuitive errors grew with model size in the GPT-3 family, then vanished in ChatGPT and GPT-4. Reasoning aloud cut the trap rate.
numbers: CRT: humans 38-41% correct. GPT-3-davinci family 70-90% intuitive answers vs 55% humans. Task set: correct 5% (davinci-003) vs 59% (ChatGPT-3.5) vs 96% (GPT-4) vs 38% humans. Intuitive 80% (davinci-003) vs 15% / 0% vs 55% humans. 'Let's use algebra' suffix: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. Forcing a short answer: ChatGPT-3.5 correct unchanged (-4%), GPT-4 correct 95% to 88%.
limits: CRT is on the web and may be memorised. Tasks are about intuition traps, not anchoring or framing.
agent_relevance: Reasoning before answering helps weak models; the best models barely need the push on textbook traps.

source: Suri et al. (2024) Do large language models show decision heuristics similar to humans? (GPT-3.5 case study)
finding: ChatGPT showed anchoring, the conjunction fallacy, framing and endowment effects, with strengths similar to humans.
numbers: Anchoring: low anchor 20.83 (SE 3.38) vs human 22.50; high anchor 105.97 vs human 80.50; t(58)=8.78 for ChatGPT, 5.55 for humans. Linda: ChatGPT chose conjunction 18 of 20 (humans 85%). Framing: human ratings 5.2 vs 4.6 (t(80)=3.86). ChatGPT-4 tested on ten anchoring trials only.
limits: GPT-3.5, 30 per cell; the Linda result is a famous item.
agent_relevance: Textbook biases appear in chat models, but the samples are small and old.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Framing and anchoring-type order effects appear in high-stakes admissions prompts. Self-debiasing (the model rewrites the prompt) works better than few-shot examples.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students in the reject framing. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Selfhelp left 0% biased framing prompts (Llama 2 13B), 1.4% (7B), 2.7% (GPT-4). Few-shot debiasing sometimes drove the admit rate to 0 or 1. For anchoring, Llama models changed 40-52% of decisions when allowed to reconsider.
limits: Admissions task only; the metric is inconsistency across prompt variants, not ground-truth error.
agent_relevance: Have code strip or neutralise frames before the model sees them. Self-rewrite works for strong models only.

source: Lou & Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models
finding: GPT-4 and GPT-4o are pulled by numeric hints. Chain-of-thought, a principles prompt, 'ignore the anchor' and reflection did not fix it. Showing both a high and a low hint helped.
numbers: 62 questions with three hint types (fact, expert opinion, irrelevant). Anchor differences stayed significant (very small p) under CoT, principles, ignore and reflection in GPT-4 and GPT-4o. The 'both anchors' strategy brought GPT-4 close to the unbiased value on 8 of 15 expert-hint questions.
limits: Dataset from an earlier paper, t-tests on a modest number of items; not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Do not tell the model to ignore a number. Give two opposed references or none.

source: Itzhak et al. (2024) Instructed to bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increase decoy, certainty and belief-bias effects in models.
numbers: Models: GPT-3, Mistral, T5 families. Bias stronger in Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 than in base versions; GPT-4 partly mitigates.
limits: Abstract and discussion read; tables not read in detail. Not anchoring or framing.
agent_relevance: Tuning can add human-like bias. Measure the specific model; do not assume newer is safer.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: Seven LLMs failed H&B tasks mostly in non-human ways, and gave different answers to the same prompt.
numbers: Each task prompted ten times. GPT-4 correct with correct reasoning 69.2%; Claude 2 55.0%; Llama-2 7B incorrect 77.5%. Human-like bias in only 21.7% of GPT-3.5 answers (50.8% counting human-like correct); GPT-4 73.3% human-like overall; Llama-2 13B 8.3%; Llama-2 70B refused 41.7%.
limits: Default API settings, no system prompt. Tasks include Linda and Wason, not anchoring.
agent_relevance: LLM errors are not human biases. Debiasing aimed at human error patterns may miss them. Check consistency across samples.

source: Koo et al. (2023) Benchmarking cognitive biases in LLMs as evaluators
finding: LLM judges show order, bandwagon, salience and compassion-fade biases when comparing answers.
numbers: Abstract: about 40% of comparisons across 16 models showed bias. A bandwagon cue ('85% believe System Star is better') swayed judges.
limits: Only the abstract and first pages were read; full tables not read.
agent_relevance: Never show the judge a majority or authorship (matches guardrail G5).

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-11-01) Anchoring (cognitive bias)
finding: Secondary source for the founding numbers and the competing accounts of anchoring.
numbers: Tversky & Kahneman 1974: wheel stopped at 10 gave 25% African UN countries, at 65 gave 45%. Product task: median 512 (ascending) vs 2,250 (descending), truth 40,320. Strack & Mussweiler 1997: Gandhi age 50 vs 67. Wilson 1996: incentives and warnings did not remove the effect.
limits: Secondary. Original papers not opened. Accounts: insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility, attitude change, extremeness aversion. Page says a few clearly random anchors (die roll, random generator) failed.
agent_relevance: The founding effect is huge, but the pull comes from plausible, relevant numbers.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-11-01) Conjunction fallacy
finding: Frequency wording cuts Linda errors, but this is contested. Incentives and ability reduce but do not remove it.
numbers: Linda error 85% on probability wording; about 20% with a '100 people' frequency wording (Gigerenzer 1991). Still 57% when worded 'whether or not active in feminist movement' (T&K 1983). Cognitive ability lowers it (Oechssler 2009); real money does not remove it (Sides 2002). Tentori 2004 and Wedell & Moro 2008 found probability and frequency formats gave indistinguishable rates.
limits: Secondary source. Rival accounts: representativeness, extension neglect, conversational relevance, polysemy of 'probable' and 'and'.
agent_relevance: Ask in counted terms, in code, wherever possible.

source: Meta-analysis (OSF preprint, 2022) The effect of incentivization on the conjunction fallacy in judgments
finding: Pay for accuracy helps a little on the conjunction fallacy.
numbers: n=3,276. d=0.19, odds ratio 1.40 for a correct answer when incentivised; most variance is noise.
limits: Abstract only (via OSF API); authors not checked.
agent_relevance: Small, steady effect. Incentive-like wording in prompts is unlikely to matter much.

source: OSF preprint (2026) The role of dispositional intuitive vs deliberative thinking in classic heuristics and biases
finding: Cognitive reflection predicts availability and representativeness accuracy and adjustment from self-generated anchors. Thinking style and self-control do not.
numbers: Study 1 N=1,071 (ten cohorts). Study 2 N=480 preregistered. Bias tasks correlated only minimally with each other.
limits: Abstract only. Low correlation between bias measures argues against a single 'bias trait'.
agent_relevance: Biases are not one factor; handle each separately.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-11-01) Availability heuristic
finding: Ease of retrieval, not only count, drives availability judgments, and the effect depends on the person's uncertainty.
numbers: Schwarz 1991: recalling 6 vs 12 examples; 12 gave lower self-rated assertiveness. Vaughn 1999: effect only at semester start and for the hardest exam. Fox 2006: 2 vs 10 suggestions, the 10-suggestion group rated the course less harshly. Children aged 4-8 also show it (Geurten 2015).
limits: Secondary. Wanke 1995 offers alternative accounts; categorisation could explain the letter-K result.
agent_relevance: LLMs do not feel retrieval effort. Test list-length effects directly, not by analogy.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-11-01) Representativeness heuristic
finding: Base-rate neglect depends on perceived relevance and task format.
numbers: Tom W.: over 95% judged computer science more likely despite lower base rate. Hospital problem: 21 / 21 / 53 (larger/smaller/about the same). Taxicab: correct 41%, most subjects over 50%. Bar-Hillel & Neter: errors persisted for real-money bets.
limits: Secondary; effect sizes not given.
agent_relevance: Compute posteriors in code (G5), not by model judgment.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026-11-01) Framing effect (psychology)
finding: Asian disease problem original shares, and a note on age.
numbers: Positive frame: 72% choose the certain option; negative frame: 78% choose the risky option. Children aged 10-12 show more framing than younger children.
limits: Page lacks the 1998 meta-analysis, culture and expertise moderators.
agent_relevance: The original effect is large; modern replications are smaller (b03, b09).
